newsitem.title: USA: N. Korea seems to call off missile test-U.S..
newsitem.headline: N. Korea seems to call off missile test-U.S..

text.p: North Korea appears to have called off a planned ballistic missile test that the United States had strongly opposed as a threat to regional stability, a senior State Department official said on Thursday.

"We believe that they were making those preparations (for a medium-range missile test) and that they've now stopped the preparations," Charles Kartman, deputy assistant secretary of state for East Asian affairs, told Reuters.

Last month, the State Department said it had sent a "very strong message" to North Korea not to carry out the test for fear of stoking instability in Northeast Asia by advancing its extensive ballistic missile development programme.

Washington is also concerned over any testing that might promote North Korean missile sales to unstable areas such as the Middle East. The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency ranks the North as world's biggest exporter of ballistic missiles.

A statement on the North's state-run Central News Agency on Oct. 23 said any medium-range test was a matter of North Korean sovereignty "and no one else is entitled or has any ground to meddle with it."

Japanese defence ministry officials said in mid-October that Pyongyang had completed preparations for a test including sending a frigate into the Sea of Japan to monitor a possible missile splashdown. North Korea last test-fired a medium-range ballistic missile into waters off Japan's cost in May 1993 at a time when it was suspected of developing nuclear warheads.
Asked whether Communist-ruled North Korea had bowed to U.S. pressure, Kartman said: "I would love to believe we have that kind of influence and that is a possibility."

He added: "My best guess is that they did hear these concerns from us and from others as well and they had some second thoughts, but I don't know that those second thoughts are going to be long-lasting ones."

Kartman made his comments after addressing a symposium at the Heritage Foundation, a private research group, on the international agreement under which North Korea agreed in October 1994 to freeze its nuclear programme.

During the forum, he said the United States lacked enough information to judge whether the North Korean submariners who entered South Korean territory in September represented a trend toward a stepped-up military threat.

The submarine ran aground off South Korea on Sept. 17 as it tried to pick up three spies it had landed two days earlier, according to the only North Korean captured alive from the vessel. Of 26 North Koreans aboard the submarine, 22 were shot to death and a hunt has been under way for three missing intruders.

Kartman said the submarine incident had derailed for now prospects for getting the North to take part in proposed four-nation talks aimed at replacing the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a lasting peace.

President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed last April to bring together the two Koreas, the United States and China for the peace talks. North Korea has not yet accepted or rejected the idea.

Larry Niksch of the Congressional Research Service, an expert on East Asia, said North Korea's apparent change of heart on the missile test may show that the United States has more leverage than previously known.

"I also think that right now they do feel on the defensive because of the submarine infiltration," he said, adding that the North may regard a delay as a way of protecting the prospect of expanded dealings with the United States.
